_comment: Curriculum structure for the Academy. Data only -- no HTML, no prose beyond
the module blurb. build_academy.py renders it; verify_academy.py checks that
every `lesson` id here exists in lessons.json and that ordering is consistent
`status` is the honest state of a lesson, not a gamification lock:
published  -- the page exists and is generated
planned    -- listed in the curriculum so the shape of the course is visible,
no page generated, no dead link emitted
Spec §6 lists all ten Core lessons; all ten are published (2026-08-30).

modules.title: mTOR Core
modules.subtitle: Understand the core architecture of mTOR biology.
modules.description: Ten lessons that build the mental model most mTOR papers assume you already have: what the kinase integrates, why it works as two different complexes, how a small GTPase and its brake decide when it fires, and where the field's own evidence stops.

parts.title: The machine
parts.question: What is this kinase, and what switches it on?
parts.youCanNow: tell the two complexes apart, follow a small GTPase and the brake that holds it, and say where in the cell the switch is actually thrown

parts.title: Inputs and outputs
parts.question: What does it listen to, and what does it do about it?
parts.youCanNow: trace a nutrient or a hormone from outside the cell to a readout, and say which input a single measurement leaves undecided

parts.title: Reading the evidence
parts.question: How do I tell what to believe?
parts.youCanNow: read a claim against the method behind it, name the tier of evidence it rests on, and say what the result leaves open

beforeYouStart.title: What you need first
beforeYouStart.lede: This course does not start from zero. Here is the short list of things it assumes you already know, each in one sentence, plus six questions to check yourself against. If a few of them are new, that is worth an hour somewhere else first — lesson 03 gets hard quickly.

concepts.says: A chain of amino acids folded into a shape; the shape is what lets it do a job.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up by it.
An enzyme that attaches a phosphate group to another molecule. mTOR is one.
Adding that phosphate group, which changes what the target protein does — often switching it on or off.
The fatty boundary around a cell, and around compartments inside it such as the lysosome.
A stretch of DNA carrying the instructions for one protein.
Removing or silencing a gene so its protein is missing, which is how biologists ask what that protein was doing.

checks.q: A kinase adds what to its target?
checks.a: A phosphate group. That is the whole job description.

checks.q: If a protein is phosphorylated, has it necessarily been switched on?
checks.a: No. Phosphorylation changes what a protein does; for some targets that means on, for others off. Lessons 04 and 07 show it: AKT phosphorylation of TSC2 switches a brake off.

checks.q: What is the difference between a gene and a protein?
checks.a: The gene is the instruction in DNA; the protein is the molecule built from it.

checks.q: Why would a researcher delete a gene on purpose?
checks.a: To see what stops working without it. That is the main way a protein's job gets pinned down.

checks.q: Is the lysosome inside or outside the cell?
checks.a: Inside. It is a compartment with its own membrane, and lesson 05 is about why mTOR meets its switch there.
In a dish rather than in a living animal or person. Lesson 10 is largely about how much that distinction changes what a result supports.

notNeeded: Maths beyond percentages. There is no equation in the course.
Chemistry beyond school level. No structures to draw, no mechanisms to memorise.
A prior biology course. The seven terms above are the whole entry ticket.

elsewhere.label: MITx 7.00x — Introduction to Biology: The Secret of Life
elsewhere.says: Free to audit, self-paced. Covers every term above and a great deal more.

elsewhere.label: Khan Academy — Biology library
elsewhere.says: Free, short videos. Good for filling one gap rather than taking a course.

furtherLearning.title: Free courses and lectures
furtherLearning.lede: The Academy teaches one thing, the mTOR pathway, from the studies in this Atlas. The free courses and talks below cover the ground around it: the cell biology it assumes, the signalling above it and the biology of ageing it feeds into. None of them is ours. Each one is here because it teaches something a lesson in the Academy leans on.
furtherLearning.note: There is no big online course about mTOR alone. mTOR turns up as a chapter inside courses on signalling, metabolism and ageing, so every entry says how much of it you will actually get.

levels.label: Research
levels.says: graduate level, built around reading papers

furtherLearning.certNote: Every course here can be followed for free. On edX (MITx), Coursera and FutureLearn the free track usually comes without a certificate: a verified certificate costs money, and on some courses the free access ends after a set time, so it pays to go through them in one run.
furtherLearning.pickNote: the five I would start with if you only have time for a few: one for each kind of need, from a first talk to judging a study. The rest are here for when one of them leaves you wanting more.

order.says: Four steps, about a week of evenings before the course itself.

steps.label: Michael Hall's talk, The Story of TOR
MITx 7.00x or the KAIST signalling course

order.says: Read and watch these next to the lessons they match.

steps.label: The LibreTexts chapter, next to lessons 02, 06 and 07
Sabatini's de Duve Lecture, with lesson 05
MITx 7.06.1x, for the cell biology in depth

groups.title: About mTOR itself

items.label: The Story of TOR (Target of Rapamycin)
items.says: Michael Hall found TOR in yeast in 1991. He tells the story from a soil sample taken on Easter Island to the two protein complexes that control how big cells grow. English subtitles, and the video can be downloaded.

items.label: mTOR and Nutrient Signaling
items.says: A free university textbook chapter: the two complexes, how rapamycin binds, how leucine reaches mTORC1 through sestrin and GATOR, and how energy (AMPK) and insulin (Akt and TSC2) feed in. Reads well next to lessons 02, 06 and 07.

groups.blurb: Start here if you want the pathway itself, told by the people who found it.

groups.title: More talks on mTOR

items.label: Dr. David Sabatini's Research on the mTOR Pathway
items.provider: David Sabatini · Foundation for the NIH
items.says: A three-minute introduction to the pathway from David Sabatini, who as a graduate student at Johns Hopkins co-discovered mammalian mTOR in 1994, one of three groups to report it that year. A good first thing to watch.

items.label: mTOR in Aging, Episode 1: The Role of mTOR
items.says: An interview in plain language about what mTOR does and why it keeps coming up in research on ageing. The first part of a short series.

items.label: mTOR signaling in growth and metabolism
items.says: A full-length lecture on how mTOR controls growth and metabolism, from the scientist who found TOR. The longer, more technical follow-up to his 25-minute iBiology talk.

items.label: Signaling Pathways in Cancer Symposium: David Sabatini
items.says: A symposium talk at MIT's cancer research institute, pitched at scientists. Faster and more technical than the interview, so it works best after lessons 05 and 06.

items.label: mTOR and lysosomes in growth control (3rd de Duve Lecture)
items.says: An hour-long research lecture on how mTORC1 is controlled on the surface of the lysosome, given in honour of Christian de Duve, who discovered the lysosome. Goes with lesson 05.

items.label: Regulation of growth by the mTOR pathway
items.says: Sabatini's 2013 lecture in the NIH Wednesday Afternoon series. It walks through the two mTOR complexes: mTORC1, which drives growth through S6K and is blocked by rapamycin, and mTORC2, which acts on Akt and is largely insensitive to it. Watch it next to lesson 02.

items.label: mTOR signaling in growth and metabolism (Sjöberg Prize Lecture)
items.provider: Michael N. Hall · Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
items.says: Hall's 2022 prize lecture covers the same ground as his Nobel Fest talk in less than half the time, from the yeast TOR genes to mTOR in metabolism and liver cancer. A good choice if 85 minutes is too long.

items.label: Explaining mTOR and the biology behind rapamycin
items.provider: David Sabatini and Peter Attia · The Peter Attia Drive
items.says: A ten-minute clip from a 2023 podcast, in which Sabatini explains in plain words what mTOR does and how rapamycin acts on it. The full episode runs three hours and adds Matt Kaeberlein on rapamycin and ageing. Treat the parts about dosing in people as opinion, not evidence.

groups.blurb: Eight recorded talks, from a three-minute introduction to a one-hour research lecture.

groups.title: The biology the lessons assume

items.label: MITx 7.00x Introduction to Biology: The Secret of Life
items.says: MIT's introductory biology course, taught by Eric Lander and colleagues. It needs only secondary-school biology and chemistry and covers every term on the What you need first page, and a lot more.

items.label: Basic Principles of Cell Signaling
items.cert: Free to audit · certificate is paid
items.says: How a signal travels from a receptor into the cell. The second week covers receptor tyrosine kinases and insulin signalling, the route that reaches mTORC1 through Akt, and a later week covers how cells sense oxygen and energy. mTOR is not named in the syllabus, but this is the wiring lesson 07 builds on.

items.label: MIT 7.016 Introductory Biology, lectures 20 and 21: Cell Signaling
items.says: Two lectures from MIT's first-year biology course: receptors, second messengers and kinase cascades in the first, worked examples in the second. A shorter route into signalling than a full course.

items.label: Biology 2e, chapter 9: Cell Communication
items.says: A free, openly licensed textbook chapter on how cells send and receive signals, with review questions at the end. It covers the same ground as the What you need first page in more detail.

groups.blurb: The cell biology and signalling that lesson 01 takes for granted.

groups.title: Going deeper

items.label: MITx 7.05x Biochemistry: Biomolecules, Methods, and Mechanisms
items.says: Proteins, enzymes and metabolism at MIT undergraduate level, including the amino acids, sugars and lipids that mTORC1 responds to. It expects 7.00x plus introductory and organic chemistry.

items.label: MITx 7.06.1x Cell Biology: Transport and Signaling
items.time: 6 weeks, 4 to 6 h a week, start any time
items.says: Membranes, organelles and signal transduction, always with the experiment behind each idea. Useful for lesson 05, because the lysosome is where mTORC1 gets switched on. It expects 7.00x and 7.05x.

items.label: Cellular Metabolism and Cancer: Nature or Nurture?
items.says: An MIT seminar built on reading research papers about how tumour cells change their metabolism, the Warburg effect among them. mTOR is not in the syllabus by name. It suits someone who has finished the Academy and wants practice with primary literature.

items.label: Principles of Biochemistry
items.provider: Alain Viel and Rachelle Gaudet · HarvardX (edX)
items.says: Harvard's biochemistry course: protein structure, enzymes and the main metabolic pathways and how they are regulated. An alternative to MITx 7.05x that can be started at any time.

groups.blurb: University courses for when a lesson leaves you wanting the full mechanism.

groups.title: The lysosome and autophagy
groups.blurb: mTORC1 is switched on at the lysosome and keeps autophagy in check. These talks cover that side of the story, the subject of lessons 05 and 09.

items.label: The lysosome, from trash can to control center of cell metabolism (2nd de Duve Lecture)
items.says: Ballabio's lab found TFEB, the protein that switches on the genes for new lysosomes and for autophagy, and showed that mTORC1 holds it back. This lecture pairs with Sabatini's de Duve Lecture in the section above.

items.label: Autophagy, an intracellular recycling system (Nobel Lecture)
items.says: The 2016 Nobel lecture on how Ohsumi found the autophagy genes in starving yeast cells. TOR comes up as the switch that keeps autophagy off when nutrients are plentiful. The written lecture is also available as a PDF.

items.label: Genetics Seminar Series 2020: James Hurley
items.says: A structural biologist on how the autophagy machinery starts building its double membrane, shown with protein structures and reconstitution experiments. Best after lesson 09, for someone who wants to see what the proteins downstream of mTORC1 look like.

groups.title: Ageing and nutrient sensing

items.label: Why Do We Age? The Molecular Mechanisms of Ageing
items.cert: Free for 6 weeks with limited access · certificate is paid
items.says: Telomeres, DNA damage, epigenetics and stem cells, written for a general audience. Week five covers calorie restriction and lifespan, the nutrient-sensing side of ageing where mTOR sits.

items.label: Introduction to the Biology of Aging
items.says: Written for non-scientists by researchers at the Buck Institute. It explains the idea that ageing links diseases as different as cancer, Alzheimer's disease and diabetes. The course page does not mention mTOR by name.

items.label: Can a Drug Slow Aging? The Rapamycin Story
items.provider: Matt Kaeberlein · University of Arizona College of Pharmacy
items.says: A 2026 lecture tracing how rapamycin went from a soil bacterium to lifespan studies in yeast, worms, flies, mice and dogs. Kaeberlein argues in favour of the idea, so it helps to check each claim against the evidence codes in the Atlas: most of the lifespan data come from animals.

items.label: mTOR: How Dietary Protein and Amino Acids Affect Aging and Disease Processes
items.provider: Dudley Lamming · Brain Ponderings with Mark Mattson
items.says: A 2025 conversation on how cells sense amino acids through mTORC1, and what Lamming's lab found when mice were fed less protein or fewer branched-chain amino acids. Most of the data discussed come from mice.

groups.blurb: Where mTOR meets the biology of ageing, from general-audience courses to recorded talks by researchers in the field.

groups.title: Reading the evidence
groups.blurb: How to tell a strong study from a weak one. Useful next to lesson 10 and to the evidence codes on every study in the Atlas.

items.label: Understanding Medical Research: Your Facebook Friend is Wrong
items.provider: F. Perry Wilson · Yale University · Coursera
items.cert: Free to audit · certificate is paid
items.says: How to read a health study: what an observational study can and cannot show, how randomised trials work, and what p-values and confidence intervals mean. The same questions the evidence codes in the Atlas ask of every study.

items.label: Design and Interpretation of Clinical Trials
items.provider: Janet Holbrook and Lea Drye · Johns Hopkins University · Coursera
items.cert: Free to audit · certificate is paid
items.says: How trials are designed, randomised, masked and analysed, and how to judge a published one. Useful before reading the registered trials (RT) and human studies (H) in the Atlas.

items.label: Evidence Essentials, modules 1 to 4
items.says: Short interactive modules on evidence-based medicine, randomised trials and systematic reviews, written for readers without a medical background. Modules 1 to 4 are the relevant ones here.

items.label: Let's Experiment
items.says: How to design an experiment you can trust: variables, controls, sample size, bias and replication. The course platform has closed, so individual learners use the eBook and the video playlist. Goes well with the Research Challenges.
